newsitem.title: USA: Study says Medicaid growth rate slowing.
newsitem.headline: Study says Medicaid growth rate slowing.

text.p: The growth of the Medicaid health insurance program for the poor, elderly and disabled has slowed from recent double-digit levels and should average 7.4 percent through 2002, a study said on Tuesday.
The report was sponsored by the Kaiser Commission on the Future of Medicaid and carried out by the Urban Institute.

It predicts that slower enrollment, slower growth per beneficiary and reform in Medicaid payments to some hospitals, which states had used as a funding scam to attract more federal dollars, will reduce expected program growth.
The projections, if borne out, have important implications as Congress and the White House prepare to make another try at balancing the federal budget.

Republicans crafted a balanced budget proposal last year that initially called for close to $200 billion in Medicaid reductions and would have given states expanded power to run the program under annual block grants.

Republicans scaled back their plan, but it was never enacted into law. President Clinton opposes ending the federal entitlement to Medicaid. Both the White House and Congress are poised for another try at changes in the program next year.
The Congressional Budget Office had projected that Medicaid would grow at a 9.7 percent annual rate.
If growth holds to the lower 7.4 percent rate Medicaid spending could be tens of billions of dollars less than currently projected for 1996-2002, the study's authors said.

"If these spending projections are borne out, Medicaid's contribution to the federal budget deficit will be substantially smaller than previously projected," Diane Rowland, executive director of the Kaiser Commission, said in a statement.
Rowland said lower enrollment growth could also lead to a rise of the number of Americans without any health insurance.
But some state Medicaid directors appearing at a forum to discuss the new findings said they expected Medicaid growth to be somewhat higher than the report projected.

Medicaid is funded by the states and federal government. It provides health care for about 35 million poor, elderly and disabled Americans. The program covers 25 percent of American children and pays for more than half of all nursing home care.

Republican lawmakers and governors have called for dramatic changes in the program, which eats up a huge chunk of state budgets. From 1988-1992, federal and state Medicaid spending grew at an aveage rate of 22.4 percent.
Republican lawmakers proposed giving states more control over the program by converting it into a block grant and giving governors more latitude to set eligibility.
Opponents said the changes would endanger the program, especially nursing home aid to the elderly.
